Metric overview

Source: vignettes/articles/metrics-overview.Rmd
metrics-overview.Rmd

An embedding can put the right digit next to yours and still put two whole groups much too far apart. Which of those would matter for the way you intend to use the map?

Choosing a Starting Metric

What do you want to know? Where to start
Who stayed nearby? nn_preservation() counts how many of the original neighbors each point keeps.
Do dense regions stay dense? local_radius_correlation() checks whether points with small neighborhood radii in the input still have small radii on the map.
Do distances keep their order? random_triplet_accuracy() takes a point and two others. How often does the closer one stay closer?
Can I retrieve a label? roc_auc() and pr_auc() tell you how well images of the same digit, for example, rank ahead of the other digits.
Did a patch change shape? local_procrustes() aligns the same points in both spaces. See what happened to one patch of the Swiss roll.
Can a few points dominate the map? Compare coordinate spread with fitted-scale stress. See the two digits that set the scale of an LTSA map.
Did a gap open up? gap_index() compares triangle areas. See the gap between three digits.
Can I trust an island? steadiness_cohesiveness() checks groups in both directions, without using the digit labels.
Did two classes become easier to tell apart? Compare class_pair_auc() with the fraction of points closer to their own class centroid. To check angular spread, look at the 5s as seen from the 3s.

Which metrics work on large datasets?

Around 5,000 observations, check the memory budget before constructing a distance matrix. One dense N by N double matrix takes 8 * N^2 bytes for its entries. At 5,000 rows, budget 191 MiB for one space, 381.5 MiB for a reference and one embedding, or 572 MiB for a reference and two embeddings. A single matrix grows from 7.6 MiB at 1,000 rows to 763 MiB at 10,000 and 26.8 GiB at 60,000. Allow additional memory for coordinates, copies and working storage. The practical limit depends on which metric you run and how much memory is available.

  • Distances and their ordering. Use the full coordinates and reuse a sample of pairs across embeddings for correlation, EMD, stress or a distance-band profile. Check how many pairs reach the narrowest band. For random_triplet_accuracy(), the sample size is per observation. Global distance metrics
  • Neighbors. A graph with k neighbors per row stores N * k indices. Keep the graphs from nn_preservation(..., ret_extra = TRUE) for overlap, local radii (which also need distances) and reciprocal neighbors. Brute-force search still compares every pair. For approximate search, spot-check a few queries.
  • Exact ranks. With Euclidean coordinates, exact_rank_profiles() can score a sample of queries against every candidate. It needs only one query’s ranks at a time, but scoring all queries still requires quadratic distance work. Try a query sample.
  • Label retrieval. Give roc_auc() or pr_auc() the map coordinates in coords and a sample of query_rows. Every other observation stays in the ranking. Use the same queries in each map. Compare UMAP and t-SNE on the same digits.
  • Class geometry. label_trustworthiness_continuity() checks nearest-centroid consistency for every pair of classes. class_angular_distortion_index() estimates angular distortion from sampled triplets. Here n_triplets is the total number to draw. Both work on coordinates.
  • Patches and gaps. Reuse a reference graph for local_procrustes() and fit one small alignment per point. For gap_index(), only the edges of the 2D triangulation need distances.
  • Shared neighbors. neighbor_dissimilarity() starts with sparse graphs. One popular neighbor can occur in many lists, and every pair of those lists shares that neighbor. Even the scalar score can then require space for nearly every pair of observations.

When to use a smaller dataset. nbr_pres(), trustworthiness(), continuity(), rnx_auc(), rnx_curve(), pointwise_rank_preservation() and pointwise_rnx() each take two dense distance matrices. class_pair_auc() takes one per space. If you need class-pair AUC for just two classes, select those classes before computing distances. If the full matrices exceed your budget, use the same representative subset in every space and report the candidate pool size.

For steadiness_cohesiveness(), start with a representative subset. It takes coordinates, then builds dense distance and similarity matrices and repeatedly clusters sampled groups. Jeon and colleagues introduced the measures. Quadra follows ZADU 0.5.4 for shared-neighbor and map weights. Asking for pointwise scores adds more square matrices. Fewer iterations save CPU while the dense allocations remain. The MNIST workflow ran exact coordinate ranks for all 5,000 images and used 1,000 for the group comparison. MNIST group audit

Which scores would I use to compare UMAP or t-SNE fits?

For a sweep over initializations or parameter settings, I’d start with two scores on every fit.

  1. Neighbor overlap. I use nn_preservation() at two fixed sizes, say k = c(15, 50). A map can keep the closest few images and lose its lead farther down the list. Build the input graph once for the larger size and reuse it for every fit, even when varying UMAP’s n_neighbors or t-SNE’s perplexity. Build a fresh graph for each map. At full MNIST size I’d supply an exact 2D graph from a k-d tree or use nn_method_out = "nnd" and spot-check the approximate search. The default output search is brute force.
  2. Random triplet accuracy. Two maps can keep the same neighbors and put whole groups in different places. Given an anchor and two other images, which image was closer to the anchor in the input, and is it still closer on the map? I’d start with five triplets per observation. For 60,000 rows that’s 300,000 comparisons. Draw them once with sample_triplets() and pass the same triplets to random_triplet_accuracy() for every fit. This calculation needs dense coordinates. If the input is too large to store densely, I’d stick with graph overlap.

For an initialization comparison, keep the input representation, distance metric and optimizer settings fixed. For a parameter comparison, vary the parameter of interest. Run stochastic settings over the same set of seeds and compare the paired scores. I’d want to see a difference hold up across seeds before choosing a setting on its strength.

If finding other images of the same digit is the goal, I’d also report same-digit precision at 1, 5 and 15 from the map’s neighbor lists. That answers a different question from recovering the same individual images. In the MNIST comparison, t-SNE’s same-digit lead shrank at each cutoff in all 12 pairings. MNIST fit comparison

For a closer look at the finalists, I’d run exact_rank_profiles() on the same few hundred queries against the full candidate pool. Trustworthiness penalizes distant points that turned up nearby on the map. Continuity penalizes close neighbors that moved far away. With labels, pass the map coordinates and the same query_rows to pr_auc() to check the whole ranking.

Sample queries when the full neighbor pool matters

To estimate rank preservation for the full dataset, sample the queries and keep every row of the reference and embeddings. With x and maps from the MNIST workflow, these 500 queries each rank the other 4,999 images. The mean gives each sampled query equal weight.

set.seed(42)
queries <- sample.int(nrow(x), 500)
profiles <- exact_rank_profiles(x, maps, k = 15, query_rows = queries)
vapply(profiles, function(p) mean(p$trustworthiness[, 1]), numeric(1))

Subsetting the coordinate matrices also removes candidates and changes what the ranks mean. On the same MNIST queries at k = 100, 7s retained neighbors better than 0s in the 1,000-image pool, while 0s did better in the 5,000-image pool. At k = 500 in the larger pool, 7s led again. Report the number of queries, the size of the candidate pool and k. Full-pool MNIST comparison

Local Neighborhood Preservation

nbr_pres() compares neighborhoods from exact distance matrices. nn_preservation() and nbr_pres_knn() compare nearest-neighbor graphs. All three count the fraction of neighbors retained, as in Chen and Buja.

trustworthiness() and continuity() score misplaced neighbors by their ranks. rnx_auc() summarizes rank-based neighborhood agreement over many neighborhood sizes, while rnx_curve() retains the individual scales. pointwise_rnx() gives the comparison per observation. The rank penalties are from Venna and Kaski. Lee and colleagues describe the RNX curve and its weighted summary.

To see how far the closest neighbors move in the ranking, use exact_rank_profiles() with mrre = TRUE. A first neighbor that slips to fifth counts more than a tenth neighbor that slips to fourteenth. You can follow the input neighbors into the embedding or trace the embedding’s neighbors back to the input. Lee and Verleysen’s rank errors Worked example

See the local preservation article for examples and related local diagnostics.

Local Scale Preservation

Neighbor identity does not say whether dense and sparse regions keep their relative scale. local_radius_correlation() compares the local radius around each observation in the input data and output embedding, using either the distance to the kth neighbor or the mean distance to the first k neighbors. Narayan, Berger and Cho use local radii to assess density preservation in den-SNE and densMAP.

Local Shape Preservation

local_procrustes() checks how much the same reference neighborhood changes shape after rigid alignment. It can find distortions even when all members stay together. The matched patches follow Goldberg and Ritov. Quadra uses a fixed-scale residual.

Regional Area Distortion

gap_index() locates expansion and compression in the empty triangles of a 2D embedding. Ros, Arleo and Paulovich introduced the index. Their implementation is available. MNIST example

Local Graph Diagnostics

mutual_neighbor_correlation() compares the mutual-neighbor count pattern in the input and output nearest-neighbor graphs. It asks whether points with many or few reciprocal nearest-neighbor relationships in the input graph have similar counts in the output graph. The comparison draws on drnb.

Use neighbor_dissimilarity() when the question is which pairs of observations gain or lose shared neighbors. Fujiwara and colleagues define the measure. Graph comparison

Global Distance Preservation

quadra also contains random triplet and random pair distance methods for global structure preservation:

  • random_triplet_accuracy() checks whether sampled distance orderings are preserved, as in Wang and colleagues.
  • random_pair_distance_correlation() measures Pearson or Spearman correlation between sampled input and output distances. See Becht and colleagues and drnb.
  • random_pair_distance_emd() compares sampled distance distributions using Earth Mover’s Distance, following Heiser and Lau and their code.
  • random_pair_distance_stress() compares matched sampled distances with a root mean squared difference. This comparison draws on drnb.

For these metrics, Xin and metric_in define the reference geometry.

The identity-permutation example shows which metrics notice when the same plotted positions belong to different observations. Use distance bands to compare ordering and fitted-scale stress from nearby input pairs through the entire pair sample. The rank and fitted-scale stress comparisons follow Takaeda’s benchmark. Quadra samples pairs by default.

Input and Ordering Conventions

Sampled pair and triplet metrics require dense, finite inputs; graph metrics accept the sparse inputs supported by rnndescent.

nbr_pres() includes boundary ties, exact-rank metrics break ties by column order, and supplied-graph metrics use their stored order.

Euclidean and squared Euclidean induce the same ordering but different magnitudes. This distinction affects Pearson correlation, EMD, stress, and local-scale summaries, but not neighbor, triplet, or Spearman ordering.

Label Retrieval

roc_auc() and pr_auc() rank other observations by distance from each query and treat matching labels as relevant. They require the PRROC package.

For each class pair, label_trustworthiness_continuity() asks how many observations fall closer to their own class centroid and how that fraction changes in the embedding. class_angular_distortion_index() measures changes in the angles that one class subtends from points in another. These measures come from Jeon and colleagues and Gunaratne, Kobourov and Miller, respectively. For the former, Quadra uses the unrescaled distance consistency of Sips and colleagues.

See the label retrieval article for examples and return value details.
